title: LSP: Liskov Substitution Principle
description: When a subtype really can stand in for its parent: contracts, preconditions, postconditions and the classic Rectangle/Square trap.

questions.text: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle require?

options.text: Subclasses must not override anything
Every class must have a base class
Code written against the parent type must keep working when given any subtype, without surprises
A subclass must have more methods than its parent

questions.explanation: A subtype must honour the contract callers rely on. If a caller needs to check "is this really a Square?" before using a Rectangle, the substitution failed.

questions.text: `Square` extends `Rectangle`, and setting its width also sets the height. A function sets width 5 and height 4 and expects an area of 20. What happens with a `Square`?

options.text: The area is 20 as expected
The area is 25
A compile error
The area is 16, so the subtype broke the caller's expectation

questions.explanation: The caller reasonably assumed width and height change independently. Square strengthens that rule, so substituting it breaks the code. The fix is to stop modelling it as a mutable Rectangle subtype.

questions.text: Which change to an overridden method most clearly breaks LSP?

options.text: Returning a more specific type than the parent promised
Throwing a new exception the parent never throws and callers do not expect
Adding a log line
Accepting a wider range of inputs than the parent

questions.explanation: Subtypes may weaken preconditions (accept more) and strengthen postconditions (promise more), but surprising new failure modes break callers written against the parent.

questions.text: A `ReadOnlyList` extends `List` and throws `UnsupportedOperationException` on `add`. What does this suggest?

options.text: Exceptions are not part of a contract
It is a good use of inheritance
The hierarchy is wrong: a read-only collection is not a substitutable mutable list
LSP only applies to interfaces

questions.explanation: Callers of `List` expect `add` to work. A subtype that rejects it forces `instanceof` checks. A separate read-only interface that `List` extends is the honest design.

questions.text: Which rule do preconditions follow in a LSP-compliant override?

options.text: They may be strengthened
They must throw
They must always be removed
They may only stay the same or be weakened

questions.explanation: If the parent accepted any positive number, a subtype demanding an even number would reject inputs the caller was allowed to send. Weakening is safe; strengthening is not.

questions.text: If a subclass compiles and matches the parent type's signature, it satisfies LSP.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. LSP is about behaviour, not signatures. A method can have the right types and still break the promises (ordering, side effects, invariants) that callers rely on.

questions.text: Which are practical ways to catch LSP violations?

options.text: Run the parent's contract tests against every subtype
Look for overrides that do nothing or throw "not supported"
Check that subclass names end in the parent name
Look for `instanceof` or type checks in code that takes the parent type

questions.explanation: Shared contract tests, type checks in callers and empty or throwing overrides are all symptoms that a subtype is not really substitutable. Naming conventions prove nothing.

questions.text: A `Bird` base class has `fly()`, and `Penguin` extends it and throws in `fly()`. Which fix is best?

options.text: Catch the exception in every caller
Make `Penguin` return silently
Rename `fly` to `move`
Split the hierarchy: `Bird` without `fly`, and a `FlyingBird` that adds it

questions.explanation: Model only what all subtypes can do in the base type, and put optional capabilities in a more specific type or interface. Then no caller can hold a Penguin and call fly().
